description: We are a team led by Fayzeh, a Computer Engineering student at Birzeit University, exploring lunar mission planning. Our goal is to build an interactive tool using NASA data to compare south-pole landing sites, sunlight, and Earth visibility. We bring experience in programming, networking, and project coordination. Join us to turn space data into clear decisions! We welcome skills in web development, GIS, data analysis, UI/UX, and space science.
summary:
ZENITH is an interactive lunar mission-planning prototype that helps researchers explore when and where a planned operation near the Moon’s south pole may be feasible.

Using NASA JPL Horizons Sun/Earth geometry and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO/LOLA) terrain data, ZENITH evaluates modeled solar-panel power and geometric Earth visibility against user-defined mission requirements.

Instead of simply reporting PASS or FAIL, it explains why a plan fails, compares alternative sites and start times without changing mission requirements, and tests how sensitive those alternatives are to changes in panel orientation and power output.

In our six-hour demonstration, an original plan produces only 50.2 W against a 100 W requirement. ZENITH identifies later candidates, revealing that an apparently successful plan may still have insufficient resilience under illustrative sensitivity tests.

ZENITH transforms complex NASA-derived information into transparent, evidence-linked planning comparisons. It is intended for preliminary research screening, not certified landing safety or flight operations.
details:
ZENITH — Project Details

The Challenge

Planning lunar operations near the Moon’s south pole is difficult because local terrain can obstruct sunlight and the geometric view of Earth. A location that appears suitable at one time may fail mission requirements at another.

Mission planners need to understand not only whether a candidate operation is feasible under a model, but also what causes failure and how sensitive the result is to engineering assumptions.

Our Solution

ZENITH is an interactive, explainable mission-planning research tool that allows users to:

  • Define a lunar site, start time, operation duration, maximum scheduling delay, electrical power demand, Earth-visibility requirement, and solar-panel configuration.
  • Evaluate modeled solar power and Earth-center visibility above a sampled terrain horizon.
  • Diagnose why an original operation fails.
  • Compare alternative locations and start times while preserving the original requirements.
  • Apply illustrative sensitivity tests to expose fragile decisions.
  • Explore 3D schematic visualizations, power timelines, terrain-horizon information, and downloadable decision evidence.

NASA Data and Scientific Methodology

ZENITH combines three principal NASA-derived inputs:

JPL Horizons: Sun and Earth directions, timestamps, and actual Sun distance for the studied lunar locations.

LRO/LOLA: High-resolution local elevation models and regional terrain data for estimating potential horizon obstructions.

NASA lunar site references: Coordinates and geographic information for Connecting Ridge (Site01) and Shackleton Rim (Site04).

The prototype estimates fixed-panel direct solar power from solar irradiance, Sun distance, panel area, conversion efficiency, incidence angle, and sampled terrain blocking.

The current dataset includes 745 hourly epochs per site and 1,441 five-minute epochs per site for a focused demonstration interval.

Demonstration and Results

Our reference scenario requires six hours of operation, at least 100 W of modeled power, and geometric Earth visibility.

The original plan, starting on December 21, 2026 at 00:00 UTC, has a modeled minimum of approximately 50.2 W and fails the power requirement.

A 12:40 UTC alternative reaches 100.3 W nominally, but falls to 82.5 W under an illustrative 10% output reduction and ±1° panel orientation offsets.

A later 17:45 UTC alternative produces 120.1 W nominally and 100.25 W under the same sensitivity test.

Across the evaluated five-minute candidate search, 153 preliminary starts satisfy the nominal criteria, 92 survive the smaller sensitivity profile, and none survive the wider ±5° profile.

Technical Implementation

ZENITH uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for its interactive web interface, Three.js for an explanatory 3D scene, and Python for separate numerical verification. Node.js scripts support additional testing and reproducibility.

The project preserves source records, provenance information, and documented assumptions.

A separately implemented Python calculation agreed with 8,646 modeled power calculations, demonstrating internal numerical consistency rather than independent scientific validation.

Innovation and Intended Impact

ZENITH's contribution is its transparent decision workflow: instead of hiding uncertainty behind a single success indicator, it connects candidate decisions to their requirements, NASA-derived inputs, failure explanations, and sensitivity results.

It helps users recognize when a nominally successful operation is fragile and understand the trade-off between delaying an operation and improving its modeled power resilience.

Future development includes independent terrain and coordinate-frame validation, continuous-time analysis, battery and eclipse modeling, realistic electrical and thermal losses, and ground-station radio-link assessment.

ZENITH is a preliminary screening and educational research prototype. It does not certify safe landing sites, continuous electrical availability, or operational communication links.
